title: Is it right to become a luddite?
author: Shaun Brien
summary: A Victorian senior-secondary teacher reflects on a decade of BYOD devices, prompted by Jared Cooney Horvath's The Digital Delusion, and concludes that classroom technology has mostly harmed learning. He argues that online platforms let students show work completion rather than mastery, citing Willingham's line that memory is the residue of thought. He then critiques gamified quiz tools like Kahoot on three counts: students can opt out, speed is rewarded over thought, and responsive teaching is limited. He extends the critique to adaptive apps his daughter brute-forced for in-app currency, and to students using AI to do their thinking. He allows AI a place for teacher workload and student revision, then reports that a tech-free classroom with hard-copy work and mini whiteboards keeps students focused and makes thinking visible.
points: Online learning platforms tend to produce evidence of completion rather than thought, so Brien has students work by hand in workbooks.
Kahoot-style games let students opt out, reward speed over thinking, and undermine responsive teaching.
Adaptive apps can be gamed for rewards, as his six-year-old showed, so thinking never occurs.
AI helps teachers with workload but students tend to use it to do their thinking; acceptable student uses keep the student as the thinker.
Returning to a tech-free classroom with mini whiteboards made learning visible and removed the chance to opt out.
quotes: The panacea I thought was going to create a singular focus on efficient deep learning continues to spread student attention so thin that working memory cannot possibly function effectively.
One of the biggest problems with an online learning program such as Edrolo is that it can become an administrative burden

I’m constantly coming back to Daniel Willingham’s quote that “memory is the residue of thought” and one of the biggest problems about completing learning online is that often it is the thought that is the first thing to be removed from the equation.

Issue no.2: Games often reward speed over quality. When students receive more points for answering quickly this prioritises reaction time instead of thinking time. This means that students will more often pick distractor responses because they are not willing to take the time to truly think about the question before submitting an answer.

She was brute forcing her way through each activity by just trying every available option until she was correct so that she could accumulate the in-app currency so she could buy cosmetic items to decorate in the app. Again, if memory is the residue of thought, these app are failing when it comes to ensuring that the thinking is occurring.

AI use by students exceedingly follows the method of students copying and pasting the exact work they need to complete and having AI do the thinking for them and then the student submits AI’s work as it if is their own.

Since fully returning to a tech-free classroom for the students I have noticed that it is far easier to keep students focussed on learning. Hard copy resources and constant checks for understanding on mini white boards has meant that students have no ability to opt-out of learning. Learning and thinking become visible in a way that is truly rewarding for both the students and myself.
